title: Chapter 123 — The Musket
paragraphs: During the most violent shocks of the Typhoon, the man at the Pequod's jawbone tiller had several times been flung reeling to the deck by its spasmodic motions, even though preventer tackles had been attached to it; for they were kept slack, because some play in the tiller was indispensable.

In a severe gale like this, while the ship is only a shuttlecock tossed by the blast, it is by no means uncommon to see the needles in the compasses, at intervals, go round and round. It was so with the Pequod's; at almost every shock the helmsman had noticed the whirling speed with which they spun round on the cards; it is a sight that hardly anyone can watch without some sort of unaccustomed emotion.

Some hours after midnight, the Typhoon abated so much that through the strenuous efforts of Starbuck and Stubb — one engaged forward and the other aft — the shattered remnants of the jib and fore and main-topsails were cut adrift from the spars, and went whirling away to leeward like the feathers of an albatross, which are sometimes cast to the winds when that storm-tossed bird is on the wing.

The three corresponding new sails were now bent and reefed, and a storm-trysail was set farther aft, so that the ship soon went through the water with some precision again; and the course — for the present, east-southeast — which he was to steer, if practicable, was once more given to the helmsman. For during the violence of the gale he had steered only according to its shifts. But as he was now bringing the ship as near her course as possible, watching the compass meanwhile — look! a good sign! — the wind seemed to be coming round astern; yes, the foul breeze had turned fair!

Instantly the yards were squared, to the lively song of "Ho! the fair wind! oh-ye-ho, cheerly men!" — the crew singing for joy that so promising an event should so soon have proved false the evil omens that preceded it.

In compliance with the standing order of his commander — to report immediately, at any of the twenty-four hours, any decided change in the affairs of the deck — Starbuck had no sooner trimmed the yards to the breeze, however reluctantly and gloomily, than he mechanically went below to inform Captain Ahab of the circumstance.

Before knocking at his stateroom, he involuntarily paused in front of it for a moment. The cabin lamp — taking long swings this way and that — was burning fitfully, and casting fitful shadows on the old man's bolted door, a thin one, with fixed blinds set in it in place of upper panels. The isolated, underground seclusion of the cabin made a certain humming silence reign there, though it was hooped round by all the roar of the elements. The loaded muskets in the rack were shiningly revealed, standing upright against the forward bulkhead. Starbuck was an honest, upright man; but out of Starbuck's heart, at the instant he saw the muskets, there strangely arose an evil thought — but so blended with its neutral or good accompaniments that for the moment he hardly recognized it for what it was.

"He would have shot me once," he murmured. "Yes, there's the very musket he pointed at me — that one with the studded stock. Let me touch it — lift it. Strange, that I, who have handled so many deadly lances, strange that I should shake so now. Loaded? I must see. Yes, yes; and powder in the pan — that's not good. Better spill it? Wait. I'll cure myself of this. I'll hold the musket boldly while I think. I come to report a fair wind to him. But fair how? Fair for death and doom — that's fair for Moby Dick. It's a fair wind that's only fair for that accursed fish. The very barrel he pointed at me! — the very one; this one — I hold it here; he would have killed me with the very thing I'm handling now. Yes, and he would gladly kill all his crew. Doesn't he say he will not strike his spars to any gale? Hasn't he smashed his heavenly quadrant? And in these same dangerous seas, doesn't he grope his way by mere dead reckoning of the error-ridden log? And in this very Typhoon, didn't he swear that he would have no lightning-rods? But shall this crazed old man be meekly allowed to drag a whole ship's company down to doom with him? Yes, it would make him the willful murderer of thirty men and more, if this ship comes to any deadly harm; and my soul swears this ship will come to deadly harm if Ahab has his way. If, then, he were this instant — put aside, that crime would not be his. Ha! Is he muttering in his sleep? Yes, just there — in there, he's sleeping. Sleeping? Yes, but still alive, and soon awake again. I can't stand against you, then, old man. Not reasoning, not protest, not pleading will you listen to; you scorn all this. Flat obedience to your own flat commands — that is all you breathe. Yes, and you say the men have vowed your vow; you say all of us are Ahabs. Great God forbid! But is there no other way? No lawful way? Make him a prisoner to be taken home? What! Hope to wrest this old man's living power from his own living hands? Only a fool would try it. Say he were even tied hand and foot; knotted all over with ropes and hawsers; chained down to ring-bolts on this cabin floor; he would be more hideous than a caged tiger then. I could not endure the sight; could not possibly escape his howlings; all comfort, sleep itself, priceless reason would leave me on the long, intolerable voyage. What, then, remains? The land is hundreds of leagues away, and locked-up Japan the nearest. I stand alone here on an open sea, with two oceans and a whole continent between me and the law. Yes, yes, that's how it is. Is heaven a murderer when its lightning strikes a would-be murderer in his bed, burning sheets and skin together like tinder? And would I be a murderer, then, if —" and slowly, stealthily, half looking sideways, he placed the loaded musket's end against the door.

"On this level, Ahab's hammock swings inside; his head this way. A touch, and Starbuck may survive to hug his wife and child again. Oh Mary! Mary! — boy! boy! boy! But if I don't wake you to death, old man, who can tell to what unsounded depths Starbuck's body may sink a week from today, with all the crew! Great God, where are You? Shall I? Shall I? — The wind has gone down and shifted, sir; the fore and main topsails are reefed and set; she heads her course."
"Stern all! Oh Moby Dick, I clutch your heart at last!"
These were the sounds that now came hurtling out of the old man's tormented sleep, as if Starbuck's voice had made the long-mute dream speak.

The musket, still leveled, shook against the panel like a drunkard's arm; Starbuck seemed to be wrestling with an angel. But he turned away from the door, put the death-tube back in its rack, and left.
"He's too sound asleep, Mr. Stubb; go down, and wake him, and tell him. I must see to the deck here. You know what to say."
